prompt.context: Our client is a CPG company that makes beer. They are going through a merger. Assume our client is Firm A (the acquirer) and the target is Firm B. Firm A holds 20% of the market and Firm B holds 10% of the market. A major player, Firm C, holds a leading share of the market at 45%. The rest of the market is comprised of fringe players.
prompt.question: Can you find the cost synergies in the merger, and can you discuss their relative importance?

clarifying_info.q: Do the companies share manufacturing infrastructure?
clarifying_info.a: The companies (Firms A, B, and C) each have only one major manufacturing facility.

clarifying_info.q: What brands do these companies carry?
clarifying_info.a: Each company has one major brand in each of three areas: (a) Flagship brands which are highly profitable, (b) Maintenance brands which are marginally profitable, and (c) Cash cow / 'milk' brands which are non-growth but provide a steady source of revenue.

framework: Raw Materials Purchasing: economies of scale in ingredient sourcing (e.g., hops)
Production / Manufacturing: capacity utilization, facility consolidation
Distribution: network complementarity, capacity, in-house vs. outsourced
Sales & Marketing: elimination of duplicated head-office roles, agency consolidation, brand portfolio rationalization

questions.prompt: Where do raw material synergies exist and how significant are they?
questions.guidance: Both Firm A and Firm B are already major players (20% and 10% market share), so they likely already purchase at scale. Cost savings from combined purchasing are probably minimal — acknowledge this but do not dwell on it.

Each firm has only one major manufacturing facility. Key questions: Does either firm have excess capacity that could be utilized or eliminated? Is there potential to consolidate the two facilities into one? Savings range from zero to extremely significant depending on the answers. Probe capacity utilization before quantifying.

Key questions: Are both distribution networks currently at full capacity? Do they serve different regions (complementarity that allows expanded reach)? Is distribution in-house or outsourced? Savings could range from zero to extremely significant. Highlight that regional complementarity could actually grow revenue, not just cut costs.

questions.prompt: What sales and marketing synergies exist, and how should the firm handle its brand portfolio after the merger?
questions.guidance: Two layers: (1) Tactical savings — eliminate duplicated head-office marketing roles and consolidate external agencies. (2) Strategic brand decisions — this is where the interviewer wants significant discussion. For each brand (flagship, maintenance, cash cow) of both Firm A and Firm B, there are three options: keep as-is, reposition, or terminate. Evaluation criteria: incremental revenue impact for that brand, incremental revenue impact on other brands, and cost of repositioning or closing. For flagship brands specifically, four strategic alternatives exist: (a) keep both flagship brands, (b) shut one down, (c) keep one and reposition the other, (d) combine both into a totally new brand. Each option carries different risk profiles regarding market share loss, profit loss, and customer rejection. Also note: while the merged entity repositions itself, Firm C (45% share) may opportunistically steal market share — this competitive risk must be flagged.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the strategic alternatives for managing the flagship brands after the merger, and what are the risks of each?

categories.name: Keep Both Flagship Brands
ideas: Preserves existing customer loyalty for both brands
Higher ongoing marketing costs — no consolidation savings
Potential brand cannibalization between Firm A and Firm B flagships

categories.name: Shut One Flagship Brand Down
ideas: Risk of losing customers who preferred the shut brand to Firm C
May free up shelf space and sales force attention for surviving brand

categories.name: Keep One and Reposition the Other
ideas: Differentiates the two brands to serve distinct segments
Repositioning is costly and risky — brand equity may not transfer
Window of vulnerability during transition exploitable by Firm C
Can capture different price points or consumer demographics

categories.name: Combine Both into a Totally New Brand
ideas: Highest risk: loses equity of both existing brands simultaneously
Most expensive option (new packaging, advertising, distribution re-training)
Potential to capture a larger combined audience if executed well

recommendation: The most important synergies are in sales/marketing (brand portfolio) and potentially production/distribution, depending on capacity overlap.

For the flagship brands, keeping both initially while conducting deeper consumer research is the lowest-risk starting position; repositioning or consolidation should follow once data confirms overlap or gap.
Raw material synergies are likely minimal given both firms already operate at scale.
risks: Firm C (45% market share) can aggressively pursue Firm A+B customers during any brand transition period.
Customer rejection if a beloved brand is shut down or repositioned poorly.
Integration distraction — merger execution risk across manufacturing, distribution, and sales teams simultaneously.
next_steps: Conduct capacity utilization analysis for both manufacturing facilities to size production synergies.
Map distribution networks geographically to identify overlap vs. complementarity.
Commission consumer research to understand brand loyalty and cross-brand cannibalization risk before making any flagship brand decision.
Model revenue and cost scenarios for each of the four flagship brand strategic alternatives.
